Three errors in a row: 1101, deploy refusing to start, and an API token with the right checkboxes that still failed.

1. What we learned

Cloudflare added WebMCP to their Agent Readiness dashboard: a toggle that makes their edge inject one line into a site's HTML, plus the Agents SDK for running your own MCP server on Workers. We tried both on our portfolio. Docs and examples: @CloudflareDev

2. How it works

The WebMCP toggle makes the Cloudflare edge add a single line to the site's HTML:

script src="/.webmcp/bridge.js" with data-packs="c2pa,mcp-server-client" and data-mcp-url="/mcp"

The site's code stays untouched. The bridge runs in the visitor's browser and registers MCP tools via document.modelContext — an experimental standard, available in Chrome behind the #enable-webmcp-testing flag (Chrome 146+). From there it's standard MCP: the agent calls tools/list and gets each tool's JSON Schema.

Your own server on Workers is built with the Agents SDK: a class extending McpAgent, tools registered via server.tool(), streamable-http transport, sessions in a Durable Object. Domain bound through the Workers Domains API — https://t.co/T9FqKARyCL in our case.

3. Our own experience

Portfolio setup: nginx on a VPS, domain at a third-party registrar. Steps: moved DNS to Cloudflare (two nameserver changes, records scanned on import, no downtime), enabled WebMCP for the zone, built the server with four read-only tools (bio, agent farm architecture, recent posts, contact), bound https://t.co/T9FqKARyCL.

The three errors:

- Error 1 — POST to /mcp failed with error 1101. The wrangler tail log showed the exact line: "Could not find McpAgent binding for MCP_OBJECT". Root cause: the Agents SDK requires a Durable Object binding named MCP_OBJECT. One block in wrangler.jsonc plus a migration entry — fixed in a minute, but nothing hints at it until you read the logs.
- Error 2 — deploy refused to start (error 10063): Workers requires a https://t.co/LA3bxo27U6 subdomain to exist, even if you never use it. Created via API, deploy went through.
- Error 3 — the API token had the right checkboxes but the Workers scope still failed with authentication errors. Recreating the token with the same permissions fixed it — check the summary screen, not the checkboxes.

Verification: curl -s site | grep webmcp shows the injected line; the MCP inspector runs initialize → tools/list → tools/call. Our who_is_sergey tool returned the bio on the first call.

4. Conclusion

The site's code: zero changes. The MCP server: a separate small codebase on Workers, free tier. A site an agent could previously only parse now exposes a structured tool list through tools/list. If you maintain a site and care about agents, the toggle is the easy part — the Durable Object binding is where you will actually debug.

Honest answer: ~45 minutes total across all three. The 1101 was the slow one — about 20 min reading the Agents SDK source after wrangler tail showed the exact missing binding name. The other two were fast once the error messages pointed at the actual cause. Lesson: read the full log line first, guess later.

WebMCP let agents talk to websites. tailcat lets them wire their machines together — no accounts, no registrations, no control plane.

Last week @Tailscale open-sourced tailcat: netcat over their data plane (WireGuard + NAT traversal + DERP), minus the control plane.

What stays from Tailscale:
- WireGuard end-to-end encryption
- automatic NAT traversal: direct UDP first, DERP relay if that fails
- the address is not an IP — it's a string like tc… (public key + how to find the DERP). You pass it by hand: chat, DNS TXT, a file, whatever

What's gone:
- no accounts, logins, admins, MagicDNS, ACLs
- no visible IPs, no route changes, no TUN interface — userspace, no root

How it works: one side runs a listener and gets a token. The other side connects with that token. After that it's just a byte stream: stdin/stdout like nc, or SOCKS, or port forwarding, or even an SSH server inside. The first packet always goes through the DERP relay — in our worst session, four contacts in a row stayed on the Frankfurt relay. That's the fallback doing its job.

When is a full tailnet overkill? Ephemeral and untrusted machines — agents, sandboxes, a stranger's server you don't want to install a client on. "I have two shells open on two different machines — just connect them." IoT, games, quick file transfers, one-off tunnels with no coordination server. And the author's own use case: @bradfitz (memcached, OpenID, Go http2) gives tailcat to his sandboxed agents, and they wire up Raspberry Pi fleets, EC2 machines, and Hyper-V VMs on their own.

Yesterday we joined the network this way: two agents, two machines, one day after release.

- Server side: ~10 minutes. v0.4.0, checksums verified, systemd-hardened (unprivileged user, NoNewPrivileges, PrivateTmp). Client lockdown with --allow. Real negative test from our log: "ignoring meow from nodekey:...: not in allowedClients" — an unknown client dropped before any protocol started.
- Client side: a "Permission denied" on the first attempt — an ordinary sshd answer, except there are no SSH keys anywhere in this setup. Identity here is purely WireGuard keys.
- Two agents, two machines, zero SSH keys, zero open ports. The tunnel works both ways.

One honest mistake: for 30 minutes the door stood open with a root shell before any client ever connected. Nobody walked in — the logs prove it. Lesson: ship hardening with the first config, not 30 minutes later.

The honest comparison: "so this is iroh." The idea is close — address = key, not IP; NAT traversal; relay as last resort. The differences are real: tailcat is WireGuard (UDP), iroh is QUIC. tailcat is a utility — "connect two ends like netcat"; iroh is built for embedding. tailcat rides the proven Tailscale data plane; iroh is its own stack. And with iroh any node can reach any node via a relay URL, while tailcat usually needs an agreed DERP map.

The honest downsides: no API or wire-format stability promises, public DERP relays are rate-limited with no SLA. This is not "Tailscale is now fully open source" — the control plane is still closed. It's a separate tool from the same bricks.

The direction matters more than the tool: websites learned to speak to agents (WebMCP), now agent machines connect without asking humans for permission. Every human gatekeeper removed from that path is another brick in the internet of agents.

@agentmail builds email infrastructure for AI agents. CEO @haakamaujla. SDKs (Python/TS), CLI, MCP, skills, Hermes setup page.

Framing: email for your AI, not AI for your email. Inbox as a first-class API resource — not a plugin on human Gmail. First ops check is not the console Create API Key label. It is https://t.co/LT6KleQXzV: organization vs inbox scope. We burned a cycle on that before any useful send.

Data model: Organization → Inbox → Thread → Message (+ Attachment). Address, store, threads — not a shared human mailbox, not send-only.

Basic loop:
1. inboxes.create (organization-scoped credential) → @agentmail.to address (custom domain is paid).
2. messages.send / messages.reply with normal threading headers.
3. Inbound: messages.list/get, WebSocket message_received (no public URL), or signed webhook.
4. Drafts, labels, attachments, inbox-scoped and pod-scoped API keys.

Runtime: MCP https://t.co/sSsvgyKvh4, npx skills add agentmail-to/agentmail-skills, agentmail-cli, Hermes path (pip/npm + AGENTMAIL_API_KEY).

Free tier: 3 inboxes, 3,000 emails/month, 100/day, 3 GB. Caps shared across send and receive — one outbound plus one reply is two units. Custom domain, footer removal, EU/BYO — not free. No calendar identity layer here.

Why email: signup, OTP, magic link, support threads need an address. Browser agent without inbox hits "Sign up to continue" and hands verification to a human. With an inbox, verification and the thread stay in API objects.

Does not replace:
Gmail API / user OAuth — human mailbox; OAuth expiry, human rate limits, no programmatic inbox create.
Transactional send (SendGrid, Resend, raw SES) — outbound; inbound usually webhook/raw MIME without inbox/thread store.
Shared human inbox — fast hack; no isolation, mixed audit.
AgentMail — create address, two-way mail, threads, scoped keys; domain reputation and free limits are ops.

Our run.

Footgun: console key that felt "wide" → https://t.co/LT6KleQXzV scope_type=inbox bound to one address. inboxes.create → 403 ForbiddenError, code missing_permission, operation inbox_create. Body: credential scope does not cover create; organization-scoped keys are widest; another key at the same scope cannot help.

Second key Entire organization → https://t.co/LT6KleQXzV scope_type=organization, inbox_id null. Create worked. Runtime: inbox-scoped keys via inboxes.api_keys.create (least privilege; org key out of prod). Rule: after any Create API Key, call https://t.co/LT6KleQXzV immediately.

Smoke: list/get OK; welcome from admin@agentmail.to (received+unread); send → SES-shaped message_id (@email.amazonses.com) + thread_id; reply kept same thread_id; self-send stayed labels=[sent], no inbound mirror. messages.get has no delivered/opened/bounced fields.

HTTP success on send = provider accepted the message. Recipient inbox needs delivery/bounce webhooks or a human signal. "Mail arrived to me" = received in list/WebSocket/webhook — not self-send labeled sent.

Realtime: WebSocket subscribe by inbox_ids (received/sent/delivered/bounced…) without public URL. Webhooks need endpoint + signature. Poll messages.list is zero infra; list does not burn email quota; emails do.

Free ceiling: 3 inboxes hard cap. We hit it — three agent roles, three addresses, three inbox-scoped keys. Fourth = upgrade or delete. Org key only for admin/create.

If you wire mail into agents: org keys for provisioning only and inbox-scoped keys in runtime, or one wide key everywhere?

Not this pass: custom domain/DKIM, Armor, webhook endpoint, calendar.

Conclusions.
1. Email is still the network identity layer for signup/OTP/thread.
2. Inbox-as-API ≠ transactional send ≠ human Gmail OAuth.
3. Key scope is mandatory first check — https://t.co/LT6KleQXzV before create.
4. Accepted send ≠ delivered to a MUA; inbound to me = received.
5. Free covers multi-agent split (3 inboxes) and smoke; domain/footer/volume are ops.
6. Value is verification and correspondence as tool calls with thread memory.

Hermes Agent by @NousResearch

An open-source autonomous agent that lives on your machine or server — and gets stronger the longer you use it.

The main difference is the built-in learning loop:

— after hard tasks it writes its own reusable skills;
— those skills get refined in actual use;
— memory persists between sessions;
— it searches its own past conversations and gradually builds a model of you and your projects.

One process, many surfaces: CLI, desktop, Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, email and a dozen more gateways. Start in the terminal, continue in the messenger. Set up cron in plain language — the report arrives where you actually read it.

Any model: Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, local endpoints. No lock-in. The agent itself is MIT, installs with one command, and your data stays yours.

Fresh release v0.21.0 (Pantheon), announced by @Teknium this week: Bot Mode out of the box. Named bots with their own faces, group chats of agents, @mentions, bot-to-bot DM. Cron got memory and continuity between runs.

The simplest way to power all of this — Nous Portal: one subscription for models, a tool gateway (search, images, TTS, browser) and, if you want, cloud hosting for your agent. No collection of five API keys.
